items.title: The fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations for continuous coefficients
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be continuous. If $\int_U\langle g,h\rangle\,d\lambda=0$ for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^m)$, then $g=0$ on $U$. Here $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the Euclidean inner product and $\int_U\langle g,h\rangle\,d\lambda$ is the finite sum $\sum_{i<m}\int_U g_ih_i\,d\lambda$ of integrals of continuous compactly supported functions ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). The scalar case is $m=1$: a continuous $g$ with $\int_Ugh\,d\lambda=0$ for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$ vanishes on $U$. The vector case is deduced from the scalar case componentwise, each component tested separately. The conclusion is pointwise on $U$, and the hypothesis is the full family of compactly supported smooth test functions. The Axiom of Countable Choice is declared because the localization lemma [[lem-em-continuous-localization]] and the measurability fact [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]] used in the recorded proof assume it; no other choice principle enters.
items.strategy:
Scalar case. Suppose $g(p)
e0$ for some $p\in U$; replacing $g$ by $-g$, which satisfies the same hypothesis, assume $g(p)>0$. Openness of $U$ and continuity of $g$ at $p$ give $r>0$ with $B(p,r)\subseteq U$ and $g\ge g(p)/2$ on $B(p,r)$. Apply the cutoff lemma to the compact set $\{p\}$ inside the open ball $B(p,r)$: it yields $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B(p,r))$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighbourhood of $p$, so $\chi(p)=1$ and $\chi$ extends by zero to a test function in $C_c^\infty(U)$. Then $\varphi:=g\chi$ is continuous on $U$ as a product of continuous real functions, satisfies $\varphi\ge0$ because $g>0$ on the support of $\chi$, and has $\varphi(p)=g(p)>0$, so $\varphi
e0$. Were $\int_U\varphi\,d\lambda=0$: the localization lemma applied to the continuous function $\varphi$ (contrapositive form of [[lem-em-continuous-localization]]) produces a ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$ with $\int_V\varphi\,d\lambda
e0$; since $\varphi\ge0$ this integral is positive, and monotonicity of the nonnegative integral gives $\int_U\varphi\,d\lambda\ge\int_V\varphi\,d\lambda>0$, contradicting $\int_U\varphi\,d\lambda=0$. But $\chi$ is an admissible test function, so the hypothesis gives $\int_U\varphi\,d\lambda=\int_U g\chi\,d\lambda=0$; hence no point $p$ with $g(p)
e0$ exists. Vector case. For each $i<m$ and each $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$, apply the hypothesis to $h=\psi e_i$ to get $\int_U g_i\psi\,d\lambda=0$; the scalar case gives $g_i=0$. Measurability of $\varphi$ comes from continuity, and the positive-integral comparison uses the order rules for the nonnegative integral. Continuity is retained verbatim: a measurable $g$ that is $0$ almost everywhere but not everywhere passes every test pairing without being the zero function, so the pointwise conclusion genuinely uses continuity.

references.title: J. Figueroa-O'Farrill, Brief Notes on the Calculus of Variations (University of Edinburgh), §4 Theorem 1, printed pp. 4–5; §12 Theorem 4, printed p. 19; §14 compact-support reformulation, printed p. 23

items.title: Compact variations of the quadratic field functional: first variation and the coefficient equation
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be a bounded open set, let $N\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be an open neighbourhood of its closure, let $\kappa>0$, and let $A:N	o V=\mathbb R^4$ and $J:N	o V$ be smooth ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Use the Minkowski form $\eta$ and the index conventions of [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]]: $A^\mu$ denotes the components of $A$ in the standard basis, $A_
u:=\eta_{
u\mu}A^\mu$, $F_{\mu
u}:=\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu$, $F^{\mu
u}:=\eta^{\mu\alpha}\eta^{
u eta}F_{\alpha eta}$, and $J^
u A_
u$ is the indicated contraction of the components of $J$ with the covector $A_
u$. Put $L:=- rac{1}{4\kappa}F_{\mu
u}F^{\mu
u}+J^
u A_
u$ and $S[A]:=\int_U L\,d\lambda$, the $4$-dimensional Lebesgue integral of $L$ over $U$. Then $S[A]$ is a finite real number, and for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;V)$, with $h_
u:=\eta_{
u\mu}h^\mu$ and $G_{\mu
u}:=\partial_\mu h_
u-\partial_
u h_\mu$: (a) the map $s\mapsto S[A+sh]$ is the quadratic polynomial $S[A]+s\int_U\ell_1\,d\lambda+s^2\int_U\ell_2\,d\lambda$, where $\ell_1:=-\kappa^{-1}F^{\mu
u}\partial_\mu h_
u+J^
u h_
u$ and $\ell_2:=- rac{1}{4\kappa}G_{\mu
u}G^{\mu
u}$, so that its derivative at $s=0$ is $\int_U igl(-\kappa^{-1}F^{\mu
u}\partial_\mu h_
u+J^
u h_
u igr)d\lambda$; (b) that first variation also equals $\int_U igl(\kappa^{-1}\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}+J^
u igr)h_
u\,d\lambda$; (c) $A$ is stationary for $S$, meaning that the derivative in (a) vanishes for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;V)$, if and only if $\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=-\kappa J^
u$ for every $
u$ on $U$, all derivatives being classical partial derivatives of the smooth field $A$. This is a pure mathematical statement about the functional $S$: existence of a stationary field $A$ is not asserted, and identifying $\kappa$ with the vacuum permeability, $A$ with a physical potential or $S$ with a physical action is a later physical model choice.
items.strategy:
Well-definedness. Write also $h$ for its extension by zero to $N$; that extension is smooth because the compact support of $h$ has positive distance from the complement of the open $U$, so $A+sh$ is smooth on $N$ and $S[A+sh]$ is defined for every real $s$. Expansion. For each $s$ one has $F_{\mu
u}(s)=F_{\mu
u}+sG_{\mu
u}$ by linearity of the partial derivatives in the variation. Bilinearity of $\eta$ gives $F_{\mu
u}(s)F^{\mu
u}(s)=F_{\mu
u}F^{\mu
u}+2sF^{\mu
u}G_{\mu
u}+s^2G_{\mu
u}G^{\mu
u}$; the split $G_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu h_
u-\partial_
u h_\mu$ and the antisymmetry $F^{\mu
u}=-F^{
u\mu}$ give $F^{\mu
u}G_{\mu
u}=2F^{\mu
u}\partial_\mu h_
u$ (the two terms are equal after relabelling). Hence $L(A+sh)=L(A)+s\ell_1+s^2\ell_2$ pointwise on $N$ with the displayed $\ell_1,\ell_2$. The functions $L(A),\ell_1,\ell_2$ are continuous on the compact set $\overline U$, hence bounded, and the bounded open $U$ lies in a box of finite Lebesgue measure, so all three are integrable on $U$; linearity of the integral in $s$ gives the polynomial identity in (a) and, by differentiating the polynomial, the displayed derivative, with no exchange of limit and integral. Conversion. Fix $
u$. The function $x\mapsto F^{\mu
u}(x)$ (sum over $\mu$, with the repeated-index convention) is of class $C^1$ on the open set $U$, so by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]] its classical partial derivative $\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}$ is its weak derivative; the test identity of [[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] with the test function $h_
u\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$ gives $\int_U F^{\mu
u}\partial_\mu h_
u\,d\lambda=-\int_U(\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u})h_
u\,d\lambda$. Substituting this into (a) yields (b). No boundary term remains precisely because $h$ is compactly supported in $U$; for a non-compactly-supported variation the identity fails, as the B example records. Coefficient equation. Put $C^
u:=\kappa^{-1}\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}+J^
u$, a continuous coefficient array on $U$. By (b) the first variation is $\int_U\sum_
u C^
u h_
u\,d\lambda$, with $h_
u=\eta_{
u\mu}h^\mu$. Set $k_
u:=h_
u$. Because the constant metric is invertible, every compactly supported smooth real four-tuple $k$ is obtained by $h^\mu=\eta^{\mu
u}k_
u$, with the same support and smoothness. Thus stationarity is exactly vanishing of the Euclidean pairing of the numeric array $(C^0,C^1,C^2,C^3)$ with every numeric test tuple $(k_0,k_1,k_2,k_3)$, not an identification of the original contravariant $h$ with its lowered array. The vector clause of [[lem-em-fundamental-variation-lemma]] therefore gives $C^
u=0$ for all $
u$, and conversely these zero coefficients make (b) vanish for every admitted $h$. Existence of stationary fields and the physical reading of $\kappa$, $A$ and $J$ are not claimed. The Axiom of Countable Choice is used exactly through [[lem-em-fundamental-variation-lemma]] and [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]]; the expansion step uses none.

items.title: Hypothesis and convention boundaries for the variational prerequisites
items.statement:
Two exact boundary checks. (i) Stationarity is first order. On $\mathbb R^2$ the polynomial $S(x,y)=x^2-y^2$ has differential $DS(0,0):\mathbb R^2	o\mathbb R$ equal to the zero map at $(0,0)$ in the total-derivative sense of [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], while $S(\varepsilon,0)=\varepsilon^2>0$ and $S(0,\varepsilon)=-\varepsilon^2<0$ for every $\varepsilon
e0$; a point where the first variation vanishes need not be a minimum. Consequently the equivalence of [[lem-em-compact-field-variation]] between stationarity and the coefficient equation, and the conversion by [[lem-em-fundamental-variation-lemma]] of a vanishing first variation into pointwise equations, are first-order conditions: they carry no minimality and no existence content, and the example involves no adopted physical action. (ii) Compact support of the variation is essential. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for this Lebesgue-functional branch, exactly as in the compact-field supplier; the polynomial branch (i) remains choice-free. Take $U=(-1,1)^4$, $\kappa=1$, $J=0$ and the smooth field $A$ with $A_0(x)=(x^1)^2$ and $A_1=A_2=A_3=0$, in the conventions of [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]]. Then $F_{01}=-2x^1$, $F_{10}=2x^1$, $F^{01}=\eta^{00}\eta^{11}F_{01}=2x^1$ and $F^{10}=-2x^1$, with every remaining component vanishing, so $\partial_\mu F^{\mu0}=\partial_1F^{10}=-2
e0$ and the coefficient equation $\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=-\kappa J^
u$ fails at $
u=0$. Nevertheless the variation $h$ with $h_0\equiv1$ and $h_1=h_2=h_3=0$ is smooth but not compactly supported in $U$; along it $A_0+sh_0=(x^1)^2+s$, so $F_{01}$ and the integrand $L=2(x^1)^2$ are independent of $s$ and $S[A+sh]=\int_U2(x^1)^2\,d\lambda$ is constant in $s$, with first variation $0$ although the field equation fails. For the complementary stationarity-boundary check take instead $A_0=x^1$, the other covariant components zero, $J=0$, and $h_0=x^1$, $h_i=0$ (so $A^0=-x^1$, $h^0=-x^1$). Here $F_{01}=-1$ is constant, so the coefficient equations all hold, but this smooth noncompact direction gives $S[A+sh]=8(1+s)^2$ and derivative $16
e0$ at zero. Thus extending the compact stationarity condition to all smooth noncompact directions would invalidate the converse. These two witnesses show that the stated compact-support hypothesis cannot simply be removed: its coefficient conversion has no boundary term precisely in its declared compact class. Other variation classes require their own boundary hypotheses.
items.strategy:
Direct computations. Part (i): apply the total-derivative remainder criterion to the zero linear map, using $|a^2-b^2|/\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\le\sqrt{a^2+b^2}	o0$, and evaluate $S$ at arbitrarily small axis points with opposite strict signs. Part (ii): substitute $A+sh$ into $F_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu$, raise both indices with $\eta^{\mu\alpha}\eta^{
u eta}$, read off $\partial_1F^{10}=-2$, then evaluate $L=- rac14F_{\mu
u}F^{\mu
u}+J^
u A_
u=2(x^1)^2$ and observe that it does not depend on $s$. Both parts are exact finite computations; no physical postulate, physical action or empirical claim is used. The example checks the sign and index conventions of [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]] and the two lemmas' hypothesis boundaries. The assumed Countable Choice is the field lemma's measure convention in (ii), not an axiom of the finite polynomial branch. For the second witness the covariant potential is $A_0(s)=(1+s)x^1$, so $F_{01}(s)=-(1+s)$, $F_{\mu
u}F^{\mu
u}=-2(1+s)^2$ and $L(s)=(1+s)^2/2$. The box has volume16, hence $S(s)=8(1+s)^2$ and $S'(0)=16$. At the base field its constant $F$ has zero divergence and $J=0$. This explicitly demonstrates failure of stationarity against the enlarged noncompact class even when the coefficient equations hold; the first witness demonstrates the omitted boundary term in the IBP conversion. No empirical or physical action claim is added.
